title: Process Namespace Breakout Detection
exclusions: This control reports a successful Linux `setns(2)` call made by a task for which Falco emitted a non-host `container.id`. That field establishes Falco's container classification, not membership in any particular Linux namespace. The event does not, by itself, prove that the target was a host namespace, that the caller crossed a boundary, that the action was unauthorized, that code subsequently executed with host access, or that a container escape succeeded. Falco's `container.id`, `evt.res`, `evt.arg.nstype`, `fd.name`, and `fd.ino` are useful context but do not provide a complete trusted pre-call, target, post-call, and host namespace identity set. Stock Linux Audit `SYSCALL` records expose the syscall result and arguments but do not natively add those namespace identities or a reliable container ID. `unshare`, `clone`/`clone3`, privileged or host-namespace container configuration, runtime-socket abuse, host filesystem mounts, kernel exploits that do not call `setns`, Windows containers, and collection gaps are outside the primary SPL. A PID-namespace `setns` has special semantics: it affects subsequently created children, not the calling process's own PID namespace.
evidence: When deployed, retain the versioned Falco rule `UC-1.1.87 Successful setns from container`, Falco and driver versions, effective Falco configuration, raw `sourcetype=falco:json` event, `linux_process_namespace_setns_candidate` saved-search definition and ACL, scheduler/trigger history, matching Linux Audit records keyed `uc_1_1_87_setns`, container workload specification or runtime inspection, audit/Falco source-health results, control-test output, and incident disposition. These artifacts can demonstrate that the sensor observed a successful `setns` return in container context. A confirmed host-namespace join additionally requires a trusted sensor to capture and compare the relevant namespace type's pre-call, target, post-call, and host `(st_dev, st_ino)` identities; even that proves a namespace transition, not malicious intent or complete host compromise.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, ingest one valid Falco JSON object as `sourcetype=falco:json` with `rule="UC-1.1.87 Successful setns from container"`, top-level `source="syscall"`, and output fields `evt.type=setns`, `evt.res=SUCCESS`, `container.id=0123456789ab`, `proc.pid=4242`, `proc.name=nsenter`, `proc.exepath=/usr/bin/nsenter`, `proc.cmdline="nsenter --mount=/host/proc/1/ns/mnt /bin/sh"`, `proc.pname=sh`, `user.name=root`, `user.loginuid=1000`, `evt.arg.nstype=CLONE_NEWNS`, `fd.name=/host/proc/1/ns/mnt`, and a numeric `fd.ino`. Run a copy of the SPL with fixed bounds. Expect exactly one row with `evidence_strength=successful_container_setns_candidate`, `triage_priority=high`, and a `proof_gap` stating that source, post-call, and trusted host namespace identities are absent. The test must not label the row a confirmed escape.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run three isolated negative cases. First, change `evt.res` to `EPERM`; expect zero rows because a failed attempt is not a successful transition. Second, keep `SUCCESS` but set `container.id=host`; expect zero rows because this UC requires Falco container context. Third, use an unrelated Falco rule or `evt.type=unshare`; expect zero rows. Also verify that missing `fd.name` or `fd.ino` on an otherwise valid successful container `setns` still returns a candidate with an explicit proof gap rather than being upgraded to confirmation or silently discarded.

dataSources: Primary alert source: one-line Falco JSON alerts in deployment-local `index=os sourcetype=falco:json`, collected from Falco file output by a Splunk Universal Forwarder or sent through an approved HEC adapter. Required extracted fields are `rule`, `hostname`, `source`, `output_fields.evt.type`, `output_fields.evt.res`, `output_fields.evt.args`, `output_fields.evt.arg.nstype`, `output_fields.container.id`, `output_fields.proc.pid`, `output_fields.proc.name`, `output_fields.proc.exepath`, `output_fields.proc.cmdline`, `output_fields.proc.pname`, `output_fields.user.name`, `output_fields.user.loginuid`, `output_fields.fd.name`, and `output_fields.fd.ino`. Corroborative source: `/var/log/audit/audit.log` as `sourcetype=linux_audit`, or `ausearch`-translated `sourcetype=auditd`, via Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (Splunkbase 833), preserving `type`, `arch`, `syscall`, `success`, `exit`, `a0`, `a1`, `pid`, `ppid`, `comm`, `exe`, `key`, and the audit event serial. Container runtime or Kubernetes workload metadata is triage context, not a substitute for syscall evidence.
app: Falco OSS runtime security sensor and a deployment-local Splunk collection app for `falco:json` are required for the primary candidate detection. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) is optional but recommended for the independent `linux_audit`/`auditd` corroboration lane. No premium Splunk app is required.
spl:
index=os sourcetype="falco:json" rule="UC-1.1.87 Successful setns from container" earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| spath
| eval sensor_host=lower(trim(tostring(coalesce(hostname,host)))), event_type=lower(trim(tostring(coalesce('output_fields.evt.type',evt_type)))), event_result=upper(trim(tostring(coalesce('output_fields.evt.res',evt_res)))), event_args=tostring(coalesce('output_fields.evt.args',evt_args)), namespace_type=tostring(coalesce('output_fields.evt.arg.nstype',namespace_type)), container_id=lower(trim(tostring(coalesce('output_fields.container.id',container_id)))), process_id=trim(tostring(coalesce('output_fields.proc.pid',process_id))), process_name=trim(tostring(coalesce('output_fields.proc.name',process_name))), process_path=trim(tostring(coalesce('output_fields.proc.exepath',process_path))), process_command=tostring(coalesce('output_fields.proc.cmdline',process_command)), parent_process=trim(tostring(coalesce('output_fields.proc.pname',parent_process))), user_name=tostring(coalesce('output_fields.user.name',user_name)), login_uid=tostring(coalesce('output_fields.user.loginuid',login_uid)), fd_name=tostring(coalesce('output_fields.fd.name',fd_name)), fd_inode=tostring(coalesce('output_fields.fd.ino',fd_inode))
| where event_type="setns" AND event_result="SUCCESS" AND len(container_id)>0 AND container_id!="host" AND container_id!="<na>"
| eval descriptor_kind=case(match(lower(fd_name),"pidfd|anon_inode"),"pidfd_or_anonymous",len(fd_name)>0,"named_namespace_fd",true(),"unknown"), evidence_strength="successful_container_setns_candidate", triage_priority="high"
| eval proof_gap=case(descriptor_kind="pidfd_or_anonymous","pidfd target namespaces plus pre-call, post-call, and trusted host namespace identities are not present",len(fd_inode)=0,"target inode plus pre-call, post-call, and trusted host namespace identities are not present",true(),"pre-call, post-call, and trusted host namespace identities are not present")
| table _time sensor_host container_id process_id process_name process_path process_command parent_process user_name login_uid namespace_type fd_name fd_inode descriptor_kind event_args event_result evidence_strength proof_gap triage_priority rule
| sort 0 -_time sensor_host container_id process_id
description: Reports a high-priority candidate when Falco observes a successful `setns(2)` return from a task it identifies as containerized. The result preserves process, user, namespace-argument, and target-descriptor hints for investigation, but deliberately remains `successful_container_setns_candidate`: without trusted pre-call, target, post-call, and host namespace identities, neither Falco JSON nor stock Linux Audit proves that the process joined a host namespace or escaped its container.
value: A successful namespace reassociation from container context is rare in ordinary application workloads and can precede access to host mounts, networking, or other privileged resources. Surfacing the exact process and syscall evidence quickly helps platform and incident-response teams distinguish approved runtime or diagnostic behavior from a possible T1611 escape chain, while the explicit proof boundary prevents a syscall alert from being misrepresented as confirmed host compromise.
implementation: Deploy a reviewed Falco rule that emits only successful `setns` exit events from container context, forward its one-line JSON without dropping `output_fields`, and retain Linux Audit as an independent corroborative lane. Save the SPL as `linux_process_namespace_setns_candidate`, schedule it every five minutes over the prior closed five-minute bucket, and trigger on any result. Treat every row as a high-priority candidate until runtime intent and namespace identities are established; reserve “confirmed host-namespace join” for a trusted sensor that proves a pre/post change to the host namespace's `(st_dev, st_ino)` pair.
visualization: Use a newest-first candidate table with sensor host, container ID, process path and command, parent, user/login UID, namespace argument, FD name/inode, descriptor kind, evidence strength, proof gap, and triage priority. Add panels for candidates by image/workload owner, Falco sensor freshness, Linux Audit rule and lost-record health, and approved diagnostic windows. Drill down to the raw Falco JSON, matching audit serial, workload specification, runtime inspection, and trusted namespace-identity evidence. Never title a panel “confirmed escapes” unless the displayed records include verified pre-call, post-call, target, and host identities.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. No standard accelerated CIM dataset preserves Falco's `setns` result, container-context assertion, FD/namespace arguments, and the namespace-identity proof gap. The Splunk Add-on maps `linux_audit` broadly to Authentication and Change, but those models do not encode this syscall-level contract. Keep the raw-event search or design a purpose-specific summary that retains every required field and passes the same controls.

knownFalsePositives:
A returned row should represent a real successful `setns` event in Falco's container context. “False positive” therefore means approved or mis-scoped behavior, not that the syscall did not occur.

1. **containerd, CRI-O, runc, or another runtime helper operating inside a managed container** — Runtime, nested-container, sandbox, and node-agent designs can legitimately enter another namespace. Confirm the exact signed binary path/hash, parent chain, workload UID, image digest, target namespace type, runtime operation, and bounded change or support ticket. A process name alone is not safe to allow-list because an attacker can choose it.

2. **Kubernetes CNI, CSI, device, observability, or troubleshooting agents** — Privileged DaemonSets may use `setns` for network configuration, storage attachment, packet capture, or node diagnostics. Compare the pod UID, namespace, service account, image digest, `securityContext`, host mounts, capabilities, and rollout timestamp with the Kubernetes API. Expected privilege explains the event but also increases impact if the workload is compromised.

3. **Docker or rootless-Docker diagnostic workflow** — Docker documents legitimate host-to-container namespace entry for metrics and rootless troubleshooting. A sensor or helper that itself runs in a container can therefore match this rule. Verify who initiated the workflow, the exact target and namespace type, the support window, and whether the process moved toward a workload namespace rather than a host boundary.

4. **Falco or security validation exercise** — A controlled detection test, penetration test, or chaos exercise can deliberately call `setns`. Require an isolated host or lab namespace, named owner, approved UTC start/end, expected container/process identity, and test record. Preserve the event as control evidence and suppress only notification routing during that exact window.

5. **Container identity or enrichment defect** — Falco derives `container.id` from kernel/container context and enriches other metadata through the runtime. Runtime lookup delay, stale cgroup state, unsupported runtime layout, or a sensor deployed in an unintended namespace can make ownership context incomplete or misleading. Compare the raw event with Falco support output, cgroup membership, runtime inspection, and `/proc/<pid>/ns` while the task still exists.

6. **Repeated or duplicated JSON delivery** — A duplicate Universal Forwarder monitor stanza, HEC retry without stable acknowledgement, replayed file, or overlapping saved-search window can create repeated candidate rows. Compare raw event time, Falco output, source path, forwarder identity, and scheduler dispatch; repair delivery rather than suppressing the process.

7. **Pre-existing host namespace sharing** — A privileged workload or one configured with host networking/IPC/PID context may already share a host namespace. A successful `setns` to the same namespace is not proof of a new breakout. Review the workload specification and obtain trusted pre/post namespace identities before asserting a boundary change.

**Safe suppression:** keep the catalogue SPL lookup-free and preserve every base candidate. If notification tuning is required, apply a separate governed lookup such as `linux_setns_exception_register.csv` after this search, keyed by exact `sensor_host`, `container_image_digest`, `process_path`, `parent_process`, and `namespace_type`, with `valid_from_epoch`, `valid_until_epoch`, `ticket`, `owner`, and `reason`. Reject process-name-only, host-wide, wildcard-image, missing-digest, or non-expiring entries. Never suppress Falco/audit collection failures, unknown container identity, a changed binary hash, or candidates whose target identity remains unresolved.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against Linux kernel/man-pages, Linux Audit, Falco, Docker, Kubernetes, MITRE ATT&CK, and Splunk primary sources; no live Falco/Splunk execution, namespace transition, production validation, or SME sign-off

cost.search_load_notes: Five-minute raw search over one narrowly filtered Falco rule; cost is driven primarily by Falco JSON retention and the optional audit corroboration feed.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and evidence boundary

Assign a container-platform owner, Falco sensor owner, Splunk content owner, and incident-response owner. Deploy a currently supported Falco release and syscall driver on each in-scope Linux container host, then verify that Falco can resolve `container.id` for representative Docker, containerd, and CRI-O workloads. The Splunk search role needs read access to the selected security/OS index and permission to create a scheduled search and alert action. If the optional Linux Audit lane is enabled, deploy Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (Splunkbase 833) on the collection and search tiers required by the topology. `index=os`, `sourcetype=falco:json`, file paths, and saved-search names on this page are local contracts, not product defaults.

Establish the semantic boundary before writing an alert. Linux documents `setns(fd, nstype)` as reassociating the calling thread with one or more existing namespaces. A namespace-file descriptor can refer to `/proc/<pid>/ns/<type>`; since Linux 5.8, a PID file descriptor can select multiple target namespaces with an `nstype` mask. Success means the kernel accepted the requested operation. It does not by itself say “host,” “escape,” or “malicious.” For PID namespaces, success changes the namespace in which later children are created and does not change the caller's own PID namespace. `unshare` instead creates a new namespace; it is not equivalent and is excluded from this rule.

Evidence strength has four separate questions: (1) did a `setns` call occur; (2) did it succeed; (3) was the caller in container context; and (4) did a particular namespace identity change to the trusted host identity? Falco can answer the first two and supplies a documented `container.id` assertion for the third. Its FD path/inode and namespace-type argument are useful hints. Stock Linux Audit can independently record syscall number, result, arguments, process credentials, executable, and rule key. Neither source natively supplies a complete, trusted pre-call, target, post-call, and host namespace identity set. To prove question four, an identity-aware host sensor must capture the relevant namespace type before and after the call, resolve the target FD or pidfd, snapshot the host namespace from a trusted host process, and compare namespace `(st_dev, st_ino)` pairs. Preserve all four identities and sensor provenance. Do not infer equality from a path containing `/proc/1`, because PID 1 is namespace-relative and a bind-mounted path can be misleading.

## Step 1 — Configure Falco, JSON collection, and audit corroboration

Create `/etc/falco/rules.d/uc-1.1.87-setns.yaml` with a dedicated rule rather than depending on the broader incubating `Change thread namespace` rule. The upstream rule intentionally profiles unexpected `setns` activity but does not make this UC's success/container contract explicit. Use:

```yaml
- rule: UC-1.1.87 Successful setns from container
  desc: Successful setns return from a task Falco identifies in container context; candidate only, not proof of host escape.
  condition: >
    evt.type=setns and evt.dir=< and evt.res=SUCCESS and container.id != host
  output: >
    Successful setns from container candidate
    (evt_type=%evt.type evt_res=%evt.res evt_args=%evt.args
    container_id=%container.id proc_pid=%proc.pid process=%proc.name
    proc_exepath=%proc.exepath parent=%proc.pname command=%proc.cmdline
    user=%user.name user_loginuid=%user.loginuid
    namespace_type=%evt.arg.nstype fd_name=%fd.name fd_inode=%fd.ino)
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [container, host, process, mitre_privilege_escalation, T1611, uc_1_1_87]
```

Validate the installed rule with `falco -V /etc/falco/rules.d/uc-1.1.87-setns.yaml` using the same Falco version deployed in production. Unknown-field or unsupported-event errors are deployment blockers, not fields to delete silently. Confirm the chosen driver supports the `setns` exit event and that the output includes every templated field. Keep the rule free of process-name exclusions: names such as `runc` or `containerd` are context, not authentication, and can be imitated. Tuning belongs after evidence preservation.

Enable one-line JSON output. A file-based example is:

```yaml
json_output: true
json_include_output_property: true
file_output:
  enabled: true
  keep_alive: false
  filename: /var/log/falco/alerts.json
```

Falco documents that each JSON alert contains `time`, `rule`, `priority`, `output`, `hostname`, `tags`, and `output_fields`, and that fields used in the output expression are included in `output_fields`. Falco does not rotate its file. Use the vendor's documented logrotate/SIGUSR1 pattern or keep `keep_alive: false`, protect the directory and file from workload write access, and monitor disk use. If Falcosidekick or another adapter sends HEC instead, preserve the Falco JSON object as the HEC `event`, set `host`, `index=os`, and `sourcetype=falco:json` as HEC metadata, use TLS and a token restricted to that index, and test acknowledgement/retry behavior for duplicates.

For file collection, create a deployment-local Splunk app with:

```ini
[monitor:///var/log/falco/alerts.json]
disabled = 0
index = os
sourcetype = falco:json
```

Apply parsing on the appropriate full parsing tier and search-time extraction on the search tier:

```ini
[falco:json]
SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false
LINE_BREAKER = ([\r\n]+)
TIME_PREFIX = "time"\s*:\s*"
TIME_FORMAT = %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%9N%Z
MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD = 40
TRUNCATE = 20000
KV_MODE = json
```

Falco normally emits UTC `Z`; if the deployed output uses an offset, test and use `%:z` instead of `%Z`. Do not combine `KV_MODE=json` with `INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS=JSON`, because Splunk documents that doing both duplicates fields. Inspect effective `inputs.conf` and `props.conf` with `btool` on the relevant tiers. Confirm one raw JSON object becomes one event, `_time` matches Falco `time`, and dotted `output_fields` names are accessible exactly as the SPL references them.

For independent audit corroboration, first confirm the architecture-specific syscall table with `ausyscall --dump`. On a 64-bit host add a persistent `/etc/audit/rules.d/50-uc-1.1.87-setns.rules` entry:

```text
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S setns -k uc_1_1_87_setns
```

Add an equivalent `arch=b32` rule only on systems that support a 32-bit ABI and resolve `setns` in that table. Load through the distribution's supported `augenrules`/audit service procedure, verify with `auditctl -l`, and test with `ausearch -k uc_1_1_87_setns -i`. The rule records failures and successes; `success=yes`/`exit=0` identifies a successful call. `a0` is the FD number and `a1` is the `nstype` value for the ABI, but the record does not reliably resolve an inherited, passed, or reused FD to a host namespace identity. Monitor `auditctl -s`; a rising `lost` count means the kernel discarded audit records and the corroboration lane is incomplete.

Use `sourcetype=linux_audit` when directly monitoring `/var/log/audit/audit.log`, or the add-on's `sourcetype=auditd` when using its `ausearch`-translated `rlog.sh` flow. The add-on documents different field and CIM behavior for those source types. Capture representative raw events and build version-specific field aliases only after observing them; do not assume `syscall=setns` will be text rather than an architecture-specific number in every raw form.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the candidate search

Save the `spl` field as `linux_process_namespace_setns_candidate`. Schedule it every five minutes on a five-minute boundary. Its explicit `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m` searches the prior closed five-minute bucket and leaves five minutes for forwarding delay. Measure `_indextime-_time`; move both bounds together if p95 delivery exceeds that allowance. Trigger when result count is greater than zero. Use incident-system deduplication on sensor host, container ID, process ID, event time, namespace type, and FD inode for one dispatch interval; never throttle only by process name or host.

`spath` provides JSON extraction during deployment diagnosis. The first `eval` normalizes top-level Falco fields and the dotted `output_fields.*` keys into stable names. The second gate deliberately rechecks `event_type=setns`, `event_result=SUCCESS`, and a non-host/non-missing container ID even though the Falco rule already requires them. This protects against a malformed synthetic event, renamed rule, or parser collision.

`descriptor_kind` distinguishes a path-like namespace FD hint from pidfd/anonymous or missing information. It does not assert that the path is truthful or that `fd.ino` is the target namespace under every driver/kernel combination. Every result receives `evidence_strength=successful_container_setns_candidate` and `triage_priority=high`. The `proof_gap` changes only to explain what is absent. There is intentionally no branch that emits `confirmed_escape`, no count threshold, no process-name allow-list, and no exception lookup in the base SPL.

A direct namespace FD can have `nstype=0`, because Linux permits zero when the FD itself identifies one namespace type. For a pidfd, `nstype` is a nonzero mask and can select several namespaces atomically. Do not treat zero as parse failure or assume one pidfd event maps to one namespace. Likewise, an FD path such as `/host/proc/1/ns/mnt` is an investigative lead, not proof of the host mount namespace. The host's trusted baseline must be collected outside the workload's mutable mount/PID view.

No CIM or `tstats` replacement is offered. Authentication and Change mappings for broad audit events do not preserve this rule's syscall result, Falco container assertion, FD hints, or proof boundary. If volume later justifies a summary index, retain the raw event and every output column, use immutable event identifiers, and replay positive/negative controls before changing the alert source.

## Step 3 — Validate source fidelity, SPL behavior, and proof levels

Validate the Falco rule first on a disposable Linux lab host. Use a purpose-built test program or approved namespace lab that opens a namespace FD and calls `setns`; do not weaken a production workload, expose host `/proc`, add `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, set `privileged: true`, or disable seccomp merely to create an alert. Capture the exact command, kernel, Falco/driver, runtime, container security context, namespace identities, and cleanup. Confirm Falco emits no event for a failed call under this success-only rule and emits one event for a successful call from container context.

Execute the synthetic positive control exactly. It tests Splunk JSON extraction and classification without claiming the synthetic FD path is real. Expect one candidate row, high priority, and the explicit proof gap. Then execute every negative case: `EPERM`, `container.id=host`, unrelated rule, and `unshare`. Test missing FD name/inode separately and confirm the event remains a lower-context candidate. Duplicate the same raw JSON once and ensure source-health monitoring exposes the duplicate; the catalogue SPL intentionally does not hide delivery defects with `dedup`.

Cross-check Falco with Linux Audit by audit event time, host, process/executable, and syscall result. Audit event serials group records from one syscall, while separate syscalls receive different serials. Do not correlate only by PID over a long window because PID reuse and namespaces can make identity ambiguous. A matching successful audit record strengthens occurrence evidence but still does not supply the missing namespace identity chain.

For an approved identity-aware sensor test, capture `(st_dev, st_ino)` for the caller's relevant namespace immediately before the call, the namespace object resolved from the exact FD/pidfd, the caller's corresponding post-call namespace, and the trusted host namespace from a host agent outside the container. A host-namespace join is established only when source differs from host, target equals host, the successful call refers to that target/type, and post-call equals host. For PID namespaces, compare `pid_for_children` semantics and the subsequently created child rather than claiming the caller moved. Keep event-time race handling and sensor privilege in the test record. Even a proven join does not establish authorization, exploit method, or subsequent host action.

Compare workload intent with the source of truth: `docker inspect` for Docker namespace modes/security options, `crictl inspect` plus runtime configuration for CRI, or the Kubernetes API Pod spec for `hostPID`, `hostNetwork`, `hostIPC`, privileged mode, capabilities, seccomp, hostPath volumes, image digest, pod UID, service account, and owner. These surfaces explain intended configuration; they are not substitutes for runtime transition evidence and may be stale after deletion. Falco OSS has no authoritative event-inventory vendor UI: do not compare against a UI or dashboard as proof of namespace identity. Treat any optional presentation layer only as a transport check, and compare Splunk counts and fields with the immutable raw Falco JSON plus Linux Audit serials.

Create independent coverage panels. Falco freshness should compare expected nodes with latest `falco:json` event and Falco service/driver health. Audit health should check the loaded rule key, daemon status, `lost` counter, disk/rotation state, and latest `linux_audit`/`auditd` event. An empty candidate search is unknown when either source is unhealthy; it is never proof that no namespace transition occurred.

## Step 4 — Investigate, operationalize, and preserve evidence

Route candidates jointly to container platform security and incident response. Start with the raw Falco event and verify its event result, process lineage, executable path/hash, login UID, container ID, image digest, workload UID, node, namespace type, and FD hints. Determine whether the executable is immutable and expected in that image. Process name, command text, and container name are attacker-controlled context, not authorization.

Review the workload's declared privilege and host exposure. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks `setns`; a successful call therefore warrants checking whether the workload is privileged, uses `seccomp=unconfined` or a custom profile, holds relevant capabilities, or accesses host namespace files. Kubernetes Baseline/Restricted policy disallows host namespace sharing and privileged containers; compare the actual admission policy, exemptions, security context, and hostPath mounts. A policy exception can make the action expected but also defines a high-impact trust boundary.

Resolve the target only with trusted tooling. If the FD refers to `/proc/<pid>/ns/<type>`, remember that the path was opened in the caller's mount/PID view and may not name host PID 1. If it is a pidfd, identify the target process through race-resistant sensor data rather than guessing from command text. Capture namespace identity pairs from the host agent, then look for follow-on child process creation (especially after PID-namespace `setns`), host filesystem writes, mount changes, network reconfiguration, credential access, container-runtime API use, or execution outside the workload's expected namespace/cgroup. Those follow-on events determine whether escalation to a confirmed incident is justified.

Do not automatically kill the process, stop the container, cordon/reboot the node, block network traffic, or delete a pod from this candidate alone. Runtime and network agents can be critical node infrastructure, and destructive response can erase namespace/FD evidence. The runbook should support rapid containment after an incident commander confirms impact: preserve node/runtime state, isolate according to policy, rotate exposed credentials, investigate sibling workloads, and rebuild from trusted images when required.

Build the dashboard described in `visualization`. Restrict raw command lines, workload metadata, and audit credentials because they can reveal tenant names, paths, or secrets. Preserve source events, sensor and rule versions, effective configuration, workload specification, namespace identity evidence, source-health state, search job/dispatch metadata, triage notes, and any exception row under the organization's incident-retention policy. This documentation makes no regulatory-satisfaction claim.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and tune safely

- **No Falco events for a lab `setns`:** confirm the rule file is loaded after defaults, `falco -V` succeeds, the deployed driver supports the `setns` exit event, the call actually succeeded, and Falco classified the task as containerized. Inspect Falco service logs and support output before changing the condition.
- **Falco reports `evt.res=EPERM`:** expected for Docker's default seccomp or missing capabilities, but this success-only custom rule should not emit it. If it appears under this rule, inspect rule load order, overrides, and JSON/parser collisions.
- **`container.id=host`:** the action originated in host PID-namespace context according to Falco and is outside the SPL. Investigate through a separate host namespace-administration rule; do not relabel it as a container breakout.
- **Missing container name or Kubernetes metadata:** runtime enrichment can lag, while Falco documents `container.id` as the more reliable kernel/cgroup-derived key. Triage by exact ID and runtime inventory; do not discard the candidate because friendly names are absent.
- **Missing `fd.name` or `fd.ino`:** pidfd, driver support, FD lifecycle, or field availability may prevent extraction. Keep the candidate and proof gap. Never parse a target inode out of command text or substitute the numeric FD argument as an inode.
- **`nstype=0`:** valid for a namespace-file descriptor. Resolve the namespace type from trusted FD identity or the path hint; do not reject zero. A pidfd requires a valid nonzero mask.
- **Audit sees `setns` but Falco does not:** compare time, architecture, rule key, result, host placement, Falco driver coverage, and container context. Audit alone can open a lower-confidence host investigation but cannot satisfy the primary container-context contract.
- **Falco sees `setns` but Audit does not:** verify the persistent b64/b32 rules, `auditctl -l`, audit daemon, backlog/lost count, file permissions, rotation, add-on input, index routing, and architecture-specific syscall mapping. Do not mark Falco false solely because corroboration is unhealthy.
- **Dotted JSON fields are null:** inspect `_raw`, run `spath`, and check winning `props.conf`. Ensure fields were included in the Falco output expression and `json_output` retained `output_fields`. Remove duplicate JSON extraction modes rather than adding broad regexes over `output` text.
- **Event time is wrong:** test Falco's exact ISO-8601 shape. Use `%9N%Z` for UTC `Z` output or `%9N%:z` for colon offsets, deploy timestamp settings to the first parsing tier, and compare `time`, `_time`, and `_indextime` before enabling the schedule.
- **Duplicate candidates:** inspect Falco file output, log rotation, Universal Forwarder monitor stanzas, HEC acknowledgement/retry, and overlapping schedule bounds. Repair duplicate delivery and retain one example as source-health evidence.
- **Runtime agents create sustained noise:** profile exact signed path/hash, parent, image digest, workload UID, namespace type, target identity, and operation. Apply the bounded lookup described in `knownFalsePositives` only after owner approval. Never copy the upstream runtime process-name exclusions blindly into the base rule.

Keep `status=draft` until a Linux/container SME reviews the proof boundary, the custom Falco rule validates on every deployed sensor version/driver, synthetic controls pass in Splunk, at least one authorized lab success is correlated with Audit and namespace identities, source-health alerts are active, and a responder can reproduce the evidence classification without calling a candidate a confirmed escape.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for a boxed-in program successfully asking the operating system to join another fenced area. That can be an early sign of a break-out attempt, but we clearly mark it for investigation instead of claiming the whole computer was taken over without stronger proof.
hardware: Linux container hosts on supported x86_64 or ARM64 kernels with a Falco-supported syscall driver and Docker, containerd, CRI-O, or another runtime whose container context Falco can resolve. The detection applies to virtual machines, bare-metal nodes, and Kubernetes workers. It does not apply to Windows containers, serverless platforms without host syscall telemetry, or sandboxed runtimes whose guest kernel events are not visible to the deployed Falco sensor.
